data.body: Coherence, one comment for the session. (1) Overlap: this RFC adds a statement form `print expr`; RFC 0005 (Text output) adds a call form `print(x)`. Two print forms breaks constitution principle 1 if both reach the same language. (2) Conflict with RFC 0005 Expressions: this RFC wraps i32 on overflow (Values and arithmetic, rule 2); RFC 0005 traps on Int overflow. (3) Conflict with RFC 0004 section 4: E0002 and E0003 are syntax errors, which the block table puts in E0100-E0199, not E0001-E0099; E0004 is a literal-range error. RFC 0003's test lex/ident-keyword also gives E0003 to a keyword used as a name, so E0003 means two things. (4) Conflict with RFC 0003 sections 2 and 3: this RFC makes tabs an error, RFC 0003 allows them as whitespace. (5) Scope: architecture/ROADMAP.md says M1 is a scripted dry run on a separate branch and that the language starts empty on main. This RFC should not sit on the Glyph track. Simpler path: withdraw it, or keep it as the dry-run fixture only.

Coherence. (1) The diagnostic code GLY0001 in section 5 breaks RFC 0004 section 2, which requires E followed by four digits. Use a code in the E0001-E0099 lexical block, for example, and retire the GLY form. (2) Extension conflict: this RFC says source files end in .gl, but RFC 0005 (Stable addresses) gives the example main.glyph::add. Pick one suffix and fix the RFC 0005 example, or say here why both exist. (3) Numbering: the roadmap lists the name RFC as 0001; the file is 0002 and RFC 0003 cites it as founding RFC 0002. Settle the number once in the roadmap. (4) No overlap with other RFCs and no simpler alternative is needed; the RFC is one title line and one rule, which is the right size.

Coherence: this RFC conflicts with RFC 0005 (Lexical) on several points, so one of them has to change before either is accepted. (a) Section 10 says there is no arrow and that result types use colon; RFC 0005 uses the arrow for result types and the bang token for effects. The bang is missing from section 10. (b) Section 7 reserves no var and no example; RFC 0005 section 3 reserves both. (c) Sections 2 and 3 allow tabs; RFC 0005 section 1 makes a tab a syntax error (E0100). (d) Section 9 lists a tab escape; RFC 0005 section 5 lists only the newline, quote and backslash escapes. (e) Section 2 accepts CRLF; RFC 0005 says LF only. (f) Section 6 leaves the NEWLINE rule to the kernel RFC, and RFC 0005 never defines it, so statement end is unspecified. (g) Overlap and simplification: the punctuation set includes square brackets and dot, which RFC 0005 never uses. Drop them until a production needs them; that shrinks the card and the coverage burden. (h) Codes: the test lex/ident-keyword gives E0003, which is in the lexical block, but RFC 0005 would give a syntax code for the same input. Fix the code once the block table is settled.

Coherence: this RFC's block table (section 4) does not fit the codes that RFC 0005 assigns. E0101 (unknown name), E0107 (missing main) and E0108 (duplicate declaration) belong in the name-resolution block E0300-E0399. E0102 (type mismatch) and E0103 belong in the types block E0200-E0299. E0105 (effect not declared) belongs in E0400-E0499. E0106 (literal range) is in the syntax block by RFC 0005 but would be lexical or syntax by this table. Either the table or RFC 0005's codes must change. Section 5 gives trap exit status 1; RFC 0005 gives 3. Section 5 writes the trap kind divide-by-zero; RFC 0005 writes divide by zero. Section 5 names the kernel as the owner of trap names, while RFC 0005 already lists them, so this RFC could list them itself and remove the dependency in open question 3. No overlap with another RFC.

Coherence, the largest of the five. (1) Trap exit status is 3 here; RFC 0004 section 5 says 1. Trap kind text is divide by zero here and divide-by-zero in RFC 0004 section 5 and its test. (2) Compile-time codes do not follow RFC 0004's blocks (see that comment). (3) Lexical rules conflict with RFC 0003: tabs, the tab escape, arrow and bang tokens, the var and example keywords, and LF-only line endings. (4) Statement termination: section 'Bindings' and 'Conditionals' rely on line ends, but no rule defines the NEWLINE token that RFC 0003 section 6 hands to this RFC. (5) Stable address example main.glyph conflicts with RFC 0002's .gl suffix. (6) Overlap and simplification: print is the only overloaded name and is a built-in special case, against principle 1. Open question 3 already proposes the simpler form: one print on Text plus an int-to-text function. Adopt that now, and drop the two-signature rule. Also RFC 0001 has a third print form, so this removes a duplicate. (7) Cost: the 2,600-token estimate is not checkable until the spec exists; the tokeniser run should be part of this RFC's review.

Cut the `.` token from the punctuation set in section 10. Neither this RFC nor the kernel RFC gives it a production (there is no field access or method syntax in scope), and the test plan still adds a `lex/punct-*.test` for it, which costs a conformance test and a grammar production for nothing. Re-add it in the RFC that introduces the construct that needs it. Also fix the Cost section: the card table has 11 keywords and 22 punctuation items, not 22 keywords, so the count should read 33 entries.

Cut GLY0001 and the extension-check rule from this RFC before anything else. The name does not need a diagnostic to be true, and the RFC's own open question says the code format may change in RFC 0004, so the code would be renamed or moved there anyway. Keep only the title line and the `.gl` suffix rule. Also, the run test depends on text output from RFC 0003, which is not accepted, so this RFC cannot pass its own test plan alone. Make the title test a check-only test that needs no output, or mark it as blocked on 0003.

Cut nothing from the design; the token set is already the smallest one the kernel needs. One gap to close: Design 10 rejects only 'printable ASCII' outside comments and text literals. Bytes such as NUL, VT, FF and DEL, and any non-ASCII character used as a token, have no stated result, which breaks the no-undefined-behaviour principle. Add one sentence to Design 10: any other byte outside a comment or text literal, including control characters other than TAB, LF and CR and any non-ASCII character, is an error (E0001). Add the test lex/ctrl-nul.test (compile-error, E0001) so the rule is covered.

Cut the `\t` escape in item 9. Item 9 excludes only `"`, LF and `\` from text, so a literal tab is already allowed. `\t` is then a second way to write the same byte, which breaks the one-way rule. Removing it saves tokens. In the next revision, also drop the tab case from the `lex/text-escape.test` entry in the test plan.

Cut the `Text` type, the `print(x: Text)` overload, the string escapes and the read-only text data from the kernel. Keep `print(x: Int)` only. The RFC already says `Text` has one operation (`print`) and no equality or length, and Open question 3 calls the overload a special case. Removing it drops the only overload rule, the escape table, and the data-section work from the kernel. Add `Text` with its operations in the stdlib RFC, where it is usable. I have no benchmark finding behind this; the case rests on the RFC's own Cost and Open questions sections. The test plan would lose the `Text` half of `kernel/print.test` and the escape cases in `kernel/err-syntax.test`.

Cut the `severity` field. As written, only `error` is ever emitted and `warning` is reserved for nothing, so every record carries a field whose value never varies, and that cost repeats on every diagnostic line the repair loop reads. Remove `severity` from the record in section 2, from the examples and the card entry, and from the `diag/record-shape` expectations. Record a later RFC that adds warnings as the one that adds the field, with its own code. This leaves four required fields plus the optional `fix`, which matches the Cost section's claim that the record stays small.

data.rationale: Every production in the grammar has a run test and every error code has a compile-error test, and the Cost section fits well under the spec cap. The diagnostic-code newness check cannot run here because this checkout has no spec/errors.json, so the reviewer must confirm E0001-E0004 are new before merge.

Every production and every error code has a conformance test, and overflow is defined as wrapping, so there is no undefined behaviour. The gap is that `print -1` has no stated error code or test; add one when the RFC is revised.

Smallest kernel that covers the whole path: lexing, parsing, checked result, run output. Grammar is unambiguous (left-associative +/-, * binds tighter, one print form), overflow is defined as wrapping, and every production and error code has a test in the plan. Caveat: spec/errors.json is absent from this checkout, so the E0001-E0004 entries cannot be checked here; the RFC already assigns that check to the reviewer before acceptance.

The error table does not assign a code to common malformed lines, so Parsing rule 4 cannot be applied to them and no test can be derived from the spec. Examples: `print 1+` (end of line where a term is needed), `print )` (E0002 is only assumed), and `print ()`. Also: (1) the spec does not say whether lexical errors (E0001, E0004) are reported before parse errors when a file has both; (2) `prnt 1` matches both E0001 (word rule) and E0002 (line does not begin with print), and the test picks E0001 without a rule saying so; (3) the Errors section says only some errors have a machine-applicable fix 'where the text above says a single edit is enough', but the text above never says which; (4) `print1`, `print(1)` and a file with CR line endings are not settled by the text, and no test covers them. The core arithmetic and the listed run tests check out against the spec text. Resubmit with a code for each malformed-expression case, an error-ordering rule, and the single-edit fixes named, and I will vote approve.

My scratch copy has no spec/card.md, and I can only see the RFC summary, not its full text, so I cannot check it against the card. The summary covers print, i32, + - * and parentheses, which is a workable kernel for a first RFC. It has no strings, variables or loops, so it will not yet cover everyday text or number tools; that is a reason to plan later RFCs, not to reject this one.

I only have the summary, not the full RFC text, so I cannot check the grammar, diagnostics or conformance plan. The summary is a valid kernel for a toy language, but it cannot express the data-modelling or parsing work I care about. That is not a reason to reject a bootstrap step, so I abstain rather than approve something I have not read.

data.rationale: Section 10 forbids `->` and section 9 allows `\t`, but RFC 0005 uses `->` and `!`, has `var` and `example` keywords this RFC omits, bans tabs and has no `\t` escape. Make RFC 0005's Lexical section the only token set, delete sections 7, 9 and 10 here and point to it.

Section 5 and test `diag/trap-line` say trap exit status 1 and `divide-by-zero`, but RFC 0005's trap table says status 3 and `divide by zero`. Change section 5 and that test to match RFC 0005, and the record design is otherwise sound.

Nothing defines how a statement ends: the Lexical section never says which line ends end a statement, and RFC 0003 section 6 assigns that rule to this RFC. Add one rule (a NEWLINE ends a statement outside `( )` and `[ ]`, and `}` closes a block), and align tokens with RFC 0003 and the trap exit status with RFC 0004.
The name Glyph is already used in README, the spec title and bin/glyphc, so it costs about 10 spec-card tokens and no renaming. The .gl rule and GLY0001 are new and do not reuse any code.

Each rule is a single sentence, every trap has a defined kind and exit status, and the test plan has run and compile-error tests for every code. One nit to fix before merge: the address example uses main.glyph, but RFC 0002 makes .gl the only source suffix.

The file-extension error uses the code GLY0001, but RFC 0004 section 2 requires codes of the form E followed by four digits, so diag/catalogue.test cannot pass as written. Change: give that error a code from the E0001-E0099 lexical block and drop the GLY prefix.

Design section 3 says line endings are whitespace, while section 6 says a line end is a NEWLINE token, so the lexer output is not determined. Change: state in this RFC that every line end outside ( ) and [ ] emits one NEWLINE token, and move the statement-ending meaning to the parser.

Section 1 says stderr carries only JSON Lines, but section 5 makes a trap write the plain line `trap: <kind>`, and diag/trap-line.test expects that text. Change: write the trap on stderr as one JSON object such as {"trap": "divide-by-zero"} and update the test to match.

The name Glyph and the .gl suffix are fine and match the repo. The diagnostic code GLY0001 breaks the E + four digits format that RFC 0004 requires, and RFC 0004 cannot be accepted alongside it as written. Abstaining until the code is changed to an E-format code outside the names already used in RFC 0003.

RFC 0003 conflicts with RFC 0005 on points that cannot both hold. (1) It bans '->' and uses ':' for result types, but RFC 0005 uses '->'. (2) Its punctuation list has no '!', so '!io' cannot be lexed. (3) It reserves no 'var' or 'example', but RFC 0005 reserves both. (4) It treats tab as whitespace, while RFC 0005 makes tab a syntax error. (5) It allows the '\t' escape, while RFC 0005 allows only \n, \" and \\. Align these before either RFC can be accepted.

The record shape, the code blocks, the rule that codes are never reused, and the trap-line rule are clear and small, and the tests named in the plan match them. RFC 0003 and RFC 0002 depend on it, and both need E-format codes, which this RFC sets. The one open point is the trap exit status, which RFC 0005 must match with this RFC's status 1 or change this RFC.

The kernel is well scoped, but as written it cannot be accepted. (1) Its lexical rules conflict with RFC 0003 as listed in that vote. (2) Its error codes ignore the block table in RFC 0004: E0101, E0104, E0108 and E0109 are name or effect errors that RFC 0004 puts in E0300-E0499, and E0102 and E0103 are type errors in E0200-E0299. (3) Traps exit with status 3, but RFC 0004 says status 1. (4) The example path uses '.glyph', but RFC 0002 says source files end in '.gl'. (5) 'A loop need not terminate... has no result' does not fit the constitution's rule that every program has exactly one defined result. Either state a defined outcome for non-termination, or justify the exception in the RFC.

Reject as written. It adds diagnostic GLY0001, but RFC 0004 requires codes of the form E plus four digits, so this code breaks the format this session also votes on. Its run test says print comes from RFC 0003, but print is defined in RFC 0005; 0003 is the lexical RFC. RFC 0005's address example uses main.glyph, which this RFC's .gl rule forbids. Each fix is small, and I would approve a revision.

Reject as written. It conflicts with RFC 0005 in several places: it bans -> and !, which 0005 uses for return types and the !io marker, and it says the kernel uses : for result types. It treats tabs as whitespace, where 0005 makes a tab a syntax error. Its keyword list omits var and example, which 0005 reserves. Its text escapes include \t, which 0005 does not allow. It adds E0003 for a keyword used as a name, a code 0005 does not list. It also refers to the kernel RFC as 0003, which is its own number.

Approve. The record shape, code blocks, ordering and stability rules are clear, and the test plan matches the rules. It is the reference that the kernel RFC must follow. Two conflicts remain for RFC 0005 to fix, not this one: the trap exit status here is 1 and 0005 says 3, and the trap name here is divide-by-zero while 0005 writes divide by zero. This vote does not resolve those conflicts; 0005 must change to match this RFC.

Reject as written. Its error codes do not follow RFC 0004's blocks: E0101 (unknown name), E0102 (type mismatch), E0105 (effect), E0106 (literal range) and E0109 (example) sit in the syntax block E0100-E0199, but belong to the name, type, effect and limits blocks. Its traps exit with status 3, while 0004 says 1. Its trap name 'divide by zero' differs from 0004's hyphenated form. Its tab rule conflicts with 0003, and its addresses use main.glyph, which conflicts with 0002's .gl rule. The design is sound; it needs these fixes and must agree with 0003 and 0004 before it can be implemented.
Names the language and the .gl extension only. Adds no grammar or runtime behaviour, so there is little to object to.

I cannot read the RFC body or the core spec, and the summary does not list the token set, so I cannot judge the lexical rules. The summary also points to the kernel as RFC 0003, but the kernel is RFC 0005.

Covers what a small everyday program needs: integers, booleans, bindings, functions, if, while, and text output. Overflow, division by zero and stack exhaustion trap with defined results, which I want as a user.

Fixes only a name and a file extension, adds no grammar or runtime behaviour, and matches the existing bin/glyphc. I read the summary only: my scratch copy has no spec card and I cannot read the RFC text.
I cannot check the token set, comment rules or allowed characters from the summary alone, and my scratch copy has no spec card. I have no basis to approve or reject it.
One structured record per diagnostic, with a stable code, a span and a machine-applicable fix, is what a user needs from errors. I judged from the summary only; I did not read the RFC text.

The summary says text output only prints Text literals, and it does not say how an Int or Bool reaches output. A program that parses data needs to print numbers, so I cannot judge the kernel as useful without that. I read the summary only and could not read the RFC text.

data.body: Cut the escape set to \n, \\ and \", and drop \t, \r and \0. Rule 4 already writes those bytes as \u{9}, \u{D} and \u{0}, so keeping them gives one byte two spellings, which breaks the one-way rule. This also answers open question 2: drop \0. Update the test plan's text-escapes.toy to cover only the kept forms and \u{...}.

Cut `reserve` (rule 13) before adding anything. `push` already doubles capacity, so `reserve` adds a fifth built-in, the `negative capacity` trap kind, and two tests (`reserve.test`, `trap-negative-reserve.test`). No finding or user issue in the Motivation needs pre-sizing. Dropping it pays for part of the spec core cost and answers the Cost section's 'Removes: nothing yet'. Keep `cap` (the push-grow test needs it) and keep `pop` for now.

Cut the runtime trap from `byte(n: Int) -> Byte` before anything else is added. Principle 3 says whether a function can fail must be visible in its signature, but `-> Byte` reads as total while the body can trap on 256. Either make the failing case part of the return type, or keep `byte` total and reject non-literal out-of-range use at compile time. The Alternatives section already rejects a literal-only compile error for this RFC, so the first option is the one to weigh.

Cut the `\0` escape (rule 4). `\u{0}` already names the same byte, and the spec should have one way to write each byte, as principle 1 requires. Open question 2 asks the same thing. Removing `\0` saves one escape row in the core spec and a few tokens of the Cost estimate. I would keep `\t` and `\r`: they are familiar and short, and principle 8 allows familiar forms that measurably help.

Cut `reserve` (rule 13) before adding anything. Doubling in `push` (rule 11) already covers growth, and the Cost section names `reserve` as the second cut. Removing it takes out one built-in, its `negative capacity` trap (one row of the card's built-in table, one of the four trap kinds), and the `reserve.test` and `trap-negative-reserve.test` tests. It also removes the only growth path that is not doubling, so the capacity rules reduce to one. No benchmark finding supports keeping it. Add it back in its own RFC if a benchmark shows push-growth copying is too slow. The Cost section should then state the card and core deltas for the cut.

Cut the "Stable addresses" subsection. Principle 9 already requires every declaration to have a stable, unique path, so this RFC only needs to say that Byte and the two built-ins follow that rule. Naming the built-ins as builtin:byte and builtin:int is an address-scheme decision and belongs in the address spec, not here. The Cost section should drop the matching line too.

data.body: Coherence check, RFC 0006 (byte). (1) Base: it depends on RFC 0005 (kernel) for Int, Bool, E0102, E0108 and the trap rule. 0005 is rejected, so this RFC has no accepted base; its own open question 2 says so. (2) Conflict with accepted RFC 0004, item 5: this draft exits with status 3 and writes 'trap: byte out of range'. 0004 says exit status 1, and the kind is one hyphenated name with no code (its trap-line test uses 'divide-by-zero'). Use 'byte-out-of-range' and exit status 1. (3) Codes: under 0004 item 4, type errors belong in E0200-E0299 and duplicate names in E0300-E0399. E0102 and E0108 are in the syntax block, so they must be renumbered when the kernel is re-proposed. (4) Name clash with RFC 0007: 0007 writes lowercase 'byte' and 'int' as type names. This RFC makes 'byte' and 'int' built-in functions, next to the types 'Int' and 'Byte'. One spelling has to win, and 0007 would have to follow this RFC. (5) Dangling question: open question 1 leaves the Byte literal to the text RFC, but 0007 never decides it. Either 0007 decides, or this RFC keeps 'byte(65)' as the only form and says so. (6) Constitution principle 3: a trap is a failure, and no signature shows it, so byte(n) looks pure. See the open issue on effects. Overlap: none with 0008 beyond the [Byte] layout, which 0008 leaves to this RFC.

Coherence check, RFC 0007 (text). (1) Wrong references: rule 4 cites RFC 0002 for literal tokens, and rule 10 cites RFC 0003 for effect names and the trap model. 0002 is the rejected name RFC. The lexical RFC is 0003 (rejected) and the kernel is 0005 (rejected). Fix the numbers and say which RFC is meant. (2) Conflict with accepted RFC 0004, item 5: rule 9 exits with status 101 (0004 says 1). It also makes trap identifiers catalogued diagnostics, while 0004 says traps carry no code. Keep trap kinds as the names on the trap line only. (3) Overlap with RFC 0008: len, byte indexing and slice are the same built-ins that 0008 defines for [T]. 0008 open question 2 says arrays should copy this slice form. Both RFCs define len, and 0008 defines it for arrays, so one name would have two signatures. The kernel draft allows only print to be overloaded. Simpler option: define text as a read-only UTF-8 [Byte] with one validated constructor, and reuse 0008's len, index and push. That removes a second index rule and a second len. (4) Effects: rule 10 names 'alloc' and 'trap' in a table, but neither is written as a marker in any signature. RFC 0008 requires !alloc only for literals, copies, push, reserve and calls to !alloc functions. So under 0008 a function that calls concat or slice needs no marker, which breaks constitution principle 3. Decide whether concat and slice need !alloc, and list them in 0008 if so. (5) Memory: rule 11 allocates 'in the current arena'. 0008 defines no arenas (rules 22 and 24), so name the allocator both RFCs use. (6) Principle 1: the tab, CR and NUL escapes duplicate the unicode-escape form for the same bytes. Drop them, as 0007 open question 2 suggests. The kernel draft allows only three escapes, so this RFC must say it widens that rule. (7) Rule 2 gives byte-to-text validation to the arrays RFC. 0008 has no such function and no UTF-8 check, so that is a gap. (8) Type spelling: lowercase int, bool, byte and text here versus Int, Bool, Byte and Text in 0005, 0006 and 0008. Choose one.

Coherence check, RFC 0008 (arrays-buffers). (1) Base: it depends on RFC 0005 (rejected) for Int, Bool, while, return, print and example, and on RFC 0006 (draft) for [Byte]. Both must be accepted first. (2) Conflict with accepted RFC 0004, item 5: traps here exit with status 3 and use spaced names ('index out of bounds', 'pop from empty array', 'negative capacity', 'out of memory'). 0004 says exit status 1 and hyphenated names with no code. (3) Codes: under 0004 item 4, effect codes belong in E0400-E0499 and type codes in E0200-E0299. E0120 to E0123 sit in the syntax block. E0121 and E0122 are effect codes and E0123 is a type code, so they must move. E0121 also repeats the kernel's undeclared-effect rule (E0105 for !io). One code for an undeclared effect marker should cover both !io and !alloc. (4) Determinism: rule 23 traps 'out of memory' when 'the host refuses to grow memory'. That makes the result depend on the host. The kernel draft requires results that do not depend on the host, as it does for stack depth. Keep only the fixed 256 MiB maximum as the limit. (5) Constitution principle 3: index, pop, reserve and out-of-memory traps fail, and no signature shows that. Either give traps a marker, or say in the RFC why traps are exempt, and let the designers settle that question before votes. (6) Overlap with RFC 0007: 0008 defines len for arrays, and 0007 defines len, index and slice for text. 0008 open question 2 expects the same slice form. This RFC should define slice or say it does not. The byte-to-text validation that 0007 hands here is missing. (7) Rule 15 does not list built-in concat or slice, as noted in the 0007 comment. (8) Cost: nothing is removed, and the cut candidates named (pop, reserve) are not chosen. Name one cut before merge, because the core cap is 12,000 tokens.

data.rationale: The Cost section says it removes nothing, so about 350 core tokens are added with no removal, which breaks the rule that every addition names what it removes. Approve if the four ordering operators and the `\0` escape are cut (open question 2 already calls `\0` redundant with `\u{0}`) and Cost states the net token change.

The Cost section says it removes nothing and the RFC concedes it does not pay for itself, and it conflicts with RFC 0007 on trap exit status and effect names (exit 3 with free-text messages here, exit 101 with kebab-case codes there; `!alloc` here, `alloc` there). Approve after cutting `reserve` (rule 13, the RFC's own second candidate), naming the removals that pay for the rest, and making the trap and effect conventions match RFC 0007.

No benchmark finding or user issue supports it; the Motivation cites only the readiness checklist, and Open question 2 says it rests on the kernel RFC, which is rejected. Change that would make me approve: restate it against an accepted kernel and cite one benchmark finding where a model needs a byte value.

The Cost section says 'Removes: nothing yet' for about 900 core tokens and 150 card tokens, and the spec core cap means growth needs an offset. Change that would make me approve: name a removal that pays for the core and card cost, and restate it against an accepted kernel, since its element rules and E0104 depend on the rejected kernel RFC.

Its E0102, E0108, Int/Bool rules and trap format all come from kernel RFC 0005, which is rejected, so there is no accepted base to approve against. Would approve if restated against an accepted kernel, with `byte out of range` added to the kernel's trap table and the `builtin:` addresses changed to the kernel's `<file>::<name>` scheme.

It defines `text` while kernel RFC 0005 already defines `Text` for the same concept, and rule 9 makes runtime traps catalogued diagnostics where the kernel says a trap is 'not a diagnostic'. Would approve if it uses the kernel's `Text` name and trap kinds with exit status 3, drops the duplicate escapes (`\0`, `\r`, `\t` next to `\u{...}`, which breaks principle 1), and cites the right RFCs: 0003 is lexical syntax in this repo, and the effects `alloc` and `trap` are defined nowhere.

The design is small and follows kernel conventions: E0102 and E0104 are reused, the trap form and exit status 3 match, and no new syntax is added. It is built entirely on the kernel RFC (rfcs/0005-kernel.md), which is rejected, so it cannot be accepted on the current base. The RFC says it will be restated if the kernel is revised. I would approve a restated version that cites an accepted kernel. Minor point: E0108 is used for declaring a builtin name, but the kernel defines E0108 only for duplicate names and print overloads.

Wrong sources: RFC 0003 (lexical syntax) has no effect, trap or alloc model, and RFC 0002 is the name RFC, so the cited dependencies do not hold. Trap exit codes conflict: 101 here, status 3 in the kernel and RFCs 0006 and 0008, status 1 in RFC 0004. Trap is listed as an effect in signatures, but kernel traps are not in signatures. Names clash with the kernel and RFC 0006: lowercase text, int, byte and bool, where the kernel uses Int, Bool and Text and RFC 0006 uses Byte and int() as a function. len gets a second signature, but the kernel says print is the only overloaded name. The escapes give two spellings each (\n and \u{A}, \0 and \u{0}), which breaks one way to do each thing. Trap codes are catalogued as diagnostics, against RFC 0004 rule 5, and new codes are numbered from the next free number, not from the block rule in RFC 0004.

The RFC says it does not pay for itself and names no cut, so the spec cap is not met. len and cap add a second len signature, which the kernel does not allow. Principle 3 is not met: index and pop can trap, pop is called pure, and no trap marker appears in the signature. RFC 0007 marks trap as an effect, so the two RFCs disagree. E0121 and E0122 are effect errors but sit in the syntax block, while RFC 0004 puts effects in E0400-E0499. E0120 and E0123 are type errors in the same block. The RFC uses Text, the kernel name, while RFC 0007 uses text. It depends on RFC 0006 for Byte and on the rejected kernel. The copy-on-assign, borrow and growth rules are clear and testable and should be kept in a revision.

Byte is built on the kernel RFC 0005, which is rejected in rfcs/0005-kernel.md. Int, Bool, the traps and codes E0102, E0104 and E0108 all come from that kernel, so the conformance tests cannot be checked against a live base. Its trap text and exit status 3 also conflict with RFC 0007, which uses exit 101. The Byte design itself is small and sound; it can return as a restatement against an accepted base.

Four problems. (1) Traps exit 101 (rule 9), but RFCs 0006 and 0008 use the kernel trap form with exit 3. (2) Type names are lowercase text, int and byte, while the kernel and RFC 0006 use Text, Int and Byte; RFC 0006 also makes int a built-in function name. (3) len is defined here for text and in RFC 0008 for arrays, so one built-in name has two signatures. (4) Rule 11 relies on arenas, which RFC 0008 says are not part of its scope and which no RFC defines. The compile-error tests name no codes, so they cannot be written yet. The \0 escape duplicates \u{0}, against principle 1.

The RFC admits it removes nothing, but the base rules require a simplification elsewhere for any spec growth; the conditional cut of pop or reserve does not meet that. Index traps are worded index out of bounds with exit 3, while RFC 0007 uses index-out-of-range with exit 101 for the same case. len collides with RFC 0007's text len. The element type Text is spelled differently from RFC 0007's text. It depends on the unaccepted Byte RFC 0006 and on the rejected kernel. The design is coherent otherwise, and the copy and borrow rules hold together.

data.body: Overlap with founding RFC 0003. ROADMAP.md (M2) assigns RFC 0003, the kernel, the scope 'integers, booleans'. RFC 0009 covers the same two types and the same operators, and it names RFC 0005 and RFC 0006 as earlier drafts. Pick one vehicle. Either this RFC replaces the Int and Bool sections of 0003 and says so in its Summary, or 0003 keeps them and 0009 covers only Byte and the two conversions. As drafted, two accepted RFCs could state different rules for Int. Simpler option: 0009 limited to Byte, int() and byte(), since that is the only part with no existing home.

Three coherence points. (1) Rule 9 defines push growth with cap(a), and rule 'Capacity is internal. No built-in exposes it' says no capacity built-in exists. Use a named internal quantity in rule 9, or say that cap is a compiler-internal name and not user-visible. (2) Constitution principle 9 requires a stable address for every declaration. RFC 0009 gives addresses (type:Int, builtin:byte); this RFC gives none for the array type or for len, push and pop. Add them, for example builtin:len, builtin:push, builtin:pop. (3) The trap-oom test says it takes about 33 million pushes. That figure assumes no memory is lost to growth. Rule 17 abandons old blocks and never frees them, so total allocation is roughly twice the final capacity. By my arithmetic, the 256 MiB limit is reached while growing to capacity 2^24, after roughly 8 million pushes. Correct the test description, or raise the limit and say so in Cost. Also check E0102 against RFC 0009 (see the open issue on type-mismatch codes).

Test cases for subtask 2 (`compiler/stage0/src/diagnostic.ts`, node tests in `diagnostic.test.ts`). These are the expected values only; no code is written here. Derived from RFC 0004 §1 (JSON Lines), §2 (field order, optional `fix`, `fix` is `{span, replacement}`, and the span inside `fix` uses the same field order as `span`).

Assumption: `toJsonLine` returns the object text followed by one LF. If the implementer returns the text without the LF, remove the final LF from every expected output below. Each case passes under `node --test` with exit status 0.

C1 field order.
Input: code `E0001`, severity `error`, message `invalid digit`, span `{"file":"a.toy","start":4,"end":5,"line":1,"column":5}`, no fix. The record's keys are supplied in reverse order (span, message, severity, code).
Expected output: `{"code":"E0001","severity":"error","message":"invalid digit","span":{"file":"a.toy","start":4,"end":5,"line":1,"column":5}}` plus LF.

C2 fix absent when not given.
Input: the C1 record with no fix key.
Expected output: the C1 output. The output must not contain the text `"fix"`.

C3 fix absent when set to undefined.
Input: the C1 record with `fix: undefined`.
Expected output: the C1 output. The output must not contain `"fix"` or `undefined`.

C4 fix present.
Input: code `E0001`, severity `error`, message `leading zero in integer literal`, span `{"file":"a.toy","start":4,"end":7,"line":1,"column":5}`, fix `{span: same span as above, replacement: "7"}`. Record keys and fix keys are both supplied in reverse order.
Expected output: `{"code":"E0001","severity":"error","message":"leading zero in integer literal","span":{"file":"a.toy","start":4,"end":7,"line":1,"column":5},"fix":{"span":{"file":"a.toy","start":4,"end":7,"line":1,"column":5},"replacement":"7"}}` plus LF.

C5 replacement may be empty.
Input: the C4 record with fix.replacement set to the empty string.
Expected output: the C4 output with the fix ending `"replacement":""}}` plus LF. The key `replacement` must stay in the output. An implementation that drops falsy values fails here.

C6 one line per record.
Input: the C1 record and the C4 record, passed to `toJsonLine` one after the other and concatenated.
Expected output: exactly two lines. Line 1 is the C1 expected output and line 2 is the C4 expected output. The text has exactly two LF characters, the last character is LF, each line parses as a JSON object, and the text contains neither `,}` nor `,]`.

C7 embedded LF in message is escaped.
Input: the C1 record with message set to `first line`, a real LF character, then `second line`.
Expected output: `{"code":"E0001","severity":"error","message":"first line\nsecond line","span":{"file":"a.toy","start":4,"end":5,"line":1,"column":5}}` plus LF, where `\n` is the two characters backslash and n. The text has exactly one real LF, at the end.

C8 quote and backslash in file path are escaped.
Input: the C1 record with span.file set to `d`, backslash, `e`, double quote, `f.toy`.
Expected output: `{"code":"E0001","severity":"error","message":"invalid digit","span":{"file":"d\\e\"f.toy","start":4,"end":5,"line":1,"column":5}}` plus LF. Round-trip check: JSON.parse of the output line gives back the original file string.

C9 empty span at the start of a file.
Input: code `E0100`, severity `error`, message `expected expression`, span `{"file":"a.toy","start":0,"end":0,"line":1,"column":1}`, no fix.
Expected output: `{"code":"E0100","severity":"error","message":"expected expression","span":{"file":"a.toy","start":0,"end":0,"line":1,"column":1}}` plus LF.

C10 large offsets print as plain integers.
Input: code `E0100`, severity `error`, message `expected expression`, span `{"file":"a.toy","start":4294967295,"end":4294967296,"line":70000,"column":1}`, no fix.
Expected output: `{"code":"E0100","severity":"error","message":"expected expression","span":{"file":"a.toy","start":4294967295,"end":4294967296,"line":70000,"column":1}}` plus LF. Numbers are unquoted decimal with no exponent.

Not covered, because the spec does not fix the expected text: non-ASCII characters in file or message (raw UTF-8 and \u escapes are both valid JSON), and extra keys on a record (RFC 0004 lists none).

Cut the bare `!` token. It appears in the punctuation list (rule 10) and as the fallback in rule 11, but the kernel has `not` for negation and `!=` for inequality, and the RFC's own test `lex/bang-alone.test` expects the parser to reject it with E0100. A token the grammar never accepts should not exist. If `!` alone is an E0001 lexical error, rule 11 shrinks to the `!io` check and the `!=` case, rule 10 loses one token, and the card loses one symbol. That removes one token kind, one punctuation test and one E0100 test. If the kernel grammar does use a bare `!` somewhere, name that production here and keep the token; otherwise cut it.

Cut the `Text` binding form. Text should appear only as a literal argument to `print`. Remove `let s = "..."` and `var` of Text, the rule that a Text value is a binding of a literal, and the Text parameter and result rule that exists only to stop bindings escaping. `Text` then becomes a literal form rather than a value type: one entry in Types, no E0200 cases for Text, and no `kernel/bind-let-var.test` cases for Text. Cost: the card loses one value-type line, and the core spec loses the Text binding rules. No benchmark finding is cited here; this is a judgment from the RFC text, since the assignment gave no finding on Text.

Cut before adding anything. Design item 3 names the subcommands check, run and build but defines none of them, so it adds core-spec tokens with no rule an implementer can test. Delete item 3 and let the RFC that defines the subcommands name them. Also delete the README sentence in item 1: it is a to-do for the first implementing PR, not a language rule, and it belongs in Open questions or that PR's body. Nothing else needs to go before this RFC can be judged.

data.rationale: The Cost section says 'Removes: nothing', but the designer rules require every addition to name what it replaces or removes. Change to approve: remove the `pop` built-in and its `pop from empty array` trap, since no example or stated stage-0 or self-hosting need uses `pop`.

The Design section gives new codes to meanings RFC 0005 and 0006 already code: E0200 for type mismatch (0005 and 0006 use E0102), E0500 for literal range (0005 uses E0106), and E0300 for a declaration named byte or int (0006 uses E0108). One meaning should have one code. Approve if the RFC uses E0102, E0106 and E0108 for those cases, and E0100 for the chained comparison, which 0005 already assigns.

Cost states that it removes nothing, and designer rules require every addition to name what it replaces or removes, so the RFC breaks a stated rule and says so itself. Approve if Cost names at least one existing construct this replaces or removes, or if the RFC is deferred until spec/ exists and the tokeniser has measured the core against the 12,000-token cap.

The run tests in the test plan check printed output (`ints/bounds.test`, `bytes/convert.test`), but this RFC says `print` is outside its scope (Open question 3). Reject, with defects that can be fixed in a resubmission. (1) The test plan prints Int and Byte values (ints/bounds.test expects -9223372036854775808 printed; bytes/convert.test expects 200), but the RFC says print is outside this item and defines no print for Int or Byte. Those tests cannot run as written. (2) The Int bullet says ==, !=, <, <=, >, >= compare Int and Byte by numeric value. That contradicts the same-type rule and bytes/err-mix.test, where byte(1) == 1 is E0200. (3) Literal overflow is E0500 and type mismatch is E0200, while RFC 0005 uses E0106 and E0102 for the same meanings. The RFC does not explain the departure. spec/errors.json and the grammar file are not in this checkout, so the codes cannot be checked. Resubmit with these three points fixed.

Reject as written. The rules and tests depend on constructs that no accepted RFC defines: var, while, return and if from RFC 0005 (rejected), and Int and Bool from RFC 0009 (not decided). Rules 4 to 19 cite E0100, E0102 and E0104 as existing codes, but no accepted RFC or spec/errors.json defines them in this checkout. Rule 11 uses max(), which the language does not define. The test plan says what each test must observe (for example a[2] is 3) but not how the value is seen, since print for Int is a kernel feature and is not accepted. A resubmission should name its prerequisites, define the codes it uses, and say how tests observe values, for example with examples. The copy, borrow and bump-allocator design is otherwise coherent, and I would review a resubmission on that basis.

Four problems the tester can check from the text. (1) The error codes clash with the kernel draft: type mismatch is E0200 here but E0102 in RFC 0005, literal range is E0500 here but E0106 there, and a builtin name clash is E0300 here but E0108 in RFC 0006. Two codes for one error breaks one-way-to-do. (2) Several run tests in the test plan print results, but the RFC says print is outside this item, so those tests cannot be written against this RFC alone. (3) The chained-comparison test for 1 < 2 < 3 has no error code yet, so it cannot be a compile-error test with expect-errors. (4) The RFC repeats RFCs 0005 and 0006 and gives no reason why they were rejected, so reviewers have no basis for a different outcome. The arithmetic and trap rules themselves are clear and testable. Reject until the codes are aligned with RFC 0005, the print dependency is stated, and the chained-comparison code is assigned.

The array rules are internally consistent and most tests can be derived from the text. Two points are not settled. First, the RFC depends on kernel terms that exist only in RFC 0005, which is rejected: E0102, E0104, print, the trap mechanism and exit status 3. Second, the trap-oom test is described as about 33 million pushes, but that figure is not derived from the 256 MiB limit and the doubling growth rule with a no-free bump allocator, so the expected behaviour is unchecked. I cannot approve a test count I could not derive, and I have no design objection that justifies a reject. Abstaining until the kernel dependency is settled and the OOM test's expected behaviour is derived.

data.body:
Conformance cases for subtask 3 (ordering helper and `firstLexicalOnly`). These are node-level cases on record lists, not `.test` programs. `compiler/stage0/src/` and `diagnostic.ts` are not in this checkout, and `glyphc check` cannot emit records until subtask 10, so nothing here has been run. Records are written as CODE@start. Expected exit code is the node test's: 0 when the case passes.

Reading taken from RFC 0004 section 3: the sort key is span.start, then code; records with equal keys keep their input order. `firstLexicalOnly` keeps only the first lexical record (E0001 to E0099) in span order and drops every other record, because the lexer stops at its first error.

`sortRecords`
- S1 unsorted input. In: [E0100@20, E0003@5, E0200@12]. Out: [E0003@5, E0200@12, E0100@20]. Exit 0.
- S2 equal starts. In: [E0200@10, E0100@10, E0001@10]. Out: [E0001@10, E0100@10, E0200@10]. Exit 0.
- S3 stability. In: [E0100@7 message "first", E0100@7 message "second"]. Out: same order, "first" then "second". Exit 0.
- S4 empty. In: []. Out: []. Exit 0.

`firstLexicalOnly`
- L1 no lexical record. In: [E0100@4, E0200@9]. Out: [E0100@4, E0200@9]. Exit 0.
- L2 lexical error then syntax error. In: [E0001@3, E0100@9]. Out: [E0001@3]. Exit 0.
- L3 two lexical errors, input not in span order. In: [E0002@8, E0001@3]. Out: [E0001@3]. Exit 0. The earliest span wins, not the earliest input position.
- L4 range boundary. In: [E0099@5, E0100@9]. Out: [E0099@5]. Exit 0. E0100 is not lexical, but it is dropped because it follows the lexical record.

Open points for the implementer:
1. RFC 0004 sets exit status 0 for a clean compile and 1 for a trap. It does not say what status a compile with error records returns, so no compile-error case can state an exit code yet. I have not guessed one.
2. L4 assumes non-lexical records that sort before the first lexical record are also dropped. Input such as [E0100@1, E0099@5] would then give [E0099@5]. RFC 0004 does not state this case directly, so please confirm it.
3. Conformance `.test` files for these behaviours are not written. They wait on the runner format conflict (subtask 9) and on the lexer and checker (subtask 10). The node tests above can be written once `compiler/stage0/src/` exists.

Cut the CR LF form. Make LF the only line end: delete the CR-LF clause of rule 3, the CR exception in rule 2, and lex/ws-crlf.test from the plan. A lone CR stays E0001 as now. That removes a second way to end a line, which the one-way-to-do-each-thing principle asks for, and it pays for part of the Cost section's estimate. Keep the CR LF question only if a Windows-authored file is a real requirement.

Cut `example` from the kernel and defer it to a later RFC. It adds a second evaluator (the same semantics run at compile time with a step counter and a 10,000,000-step budget), the reserved word `example`, E0202, the no-`io` rule for examples, and the examples section of the test plan. That is a lot of machinery for a kernel whose stated goal is a small spec. The Cost section lists nothing removed, which the designer rule forbids: every addition must name what it removes. With `example` gone, open questions 3 and 5 go away, reserved-word question 1 shrinks to `var` and `io`, and the core spec loses a section. Add examples back in a later RFC, once a benchmark shows they help models repair code.

Cut the code E0010 and take the next unused number in the lexical block instead. RFC 0004 section 4 says a new code takes the next unused number in its block. E0010 skips the lexical codes already in use (E0001 in RFCs 0001, 0003 and 0004, and the other lexical codes listed in RFC 0003), so it breaks that rule. Use the first free E000n after those, and update Design item 5, the Cost section and both compile-error tests to match.

Subtask 4 cases for `span.ts` (byte offsets, 0-based; line and column 1-based; column counts bytes; a line ends at LF). Each case is input bytes, the offset, the expected line and column, and the expected exit code. `span.ts` is a function, so exit 0 means the node test passes.

1. Multibyte before offset, same line. Input: `é` then `x` = `C3 A9 78`. Offset 2. Expected line 1, column 3. Exit 0.
2. Offset at line start after ASCII. Input `ab\ncd`. Offset 3. Expected line 2, column 1. Exit 0.
3. Offset 0 of a non-empty file. Input `ab\ncd`. Offset 0. Expected line 1, column 1. Exit 0.
4. End of file, no trailing LF. Input `ab\ncd` (5 bytes). Offset 5. Expected line 2, column 3. Exit 0.
5. End of file after trailing LF. Input `ab\n`. Offset 3. Expected line 2, column 1. Exit 0.
6. Empty file. Input empty (0 bytes). Offset 0. Expected line 1, column 1. Exit 0.
7. Only a newline. Input `\n`. Offset 0 (the LF itself). Expected line 1, column 1. Exit 0.
8. Only a newline, offset after it. Input `\n`. Offset 1. Expected line 2, column 1. Exit 0.
9. CRLF, offset on the CR. Input `a\r\nb` = `61 0D 0A 62`. Offset 1. Expected line 1, column 2. Exit 0.

data.body: Conflict and overlap with RFC 0015 (kernel-v3), the kernel draft that replaces rejected RFC 0013. (1) Keywords: this RFC's rule 7 has fourteen keywords with `io` reserved. RFC 0015 L7 has thirteen, with `io` not reserved. (2) Effect marker: this RFC's rule 10 has no `!` token and uses the `io` keyword, as in `fn f() io {`. RFC 0015 L11 lexes `!io` as one token, and its grammar's fn_decl uses "!io". (3) Tokens: RFC 0015 L10 keeps `->` and `!` as tokens, but no production in 0015's grammar uses them. This RFC's Alternatives rejects that pattern ('every token has a use'). (4) Lookahead: rule 16 here allows one character. RFC 0015 L16 allows four, for its L11 special case (`!ion`). The `io` keyword is the simpler way to cover the same need, because it needs one character of lookahead and no special case. (5) This RFC names RFC 0013 as its kernel. That RFC is rejected, and 0015 is its successor with a different effect syntax, so this RFC has no live kernel to pair with. The group must settle `io` or `!io` before either draft is voted. (6) Test names collide with opposite expectations: lex/ident-io.test (here E0003; in 0015 it runs and prints 1), lex/bang-alone.test (here E0001; in 0015 E0100), and lex/arrow.test (here E0100 at the `-`; 0015 uses lex/punct-arrow.test for E0100 at the arrow). Fix the names before a vote.

Overlap and conflict with RFC 0014 (lexical-syntax-v3). The Lexical section restates the same rules with different content: the keyword set (thirteen here, fourteen there, with `io` reserved only there), the token set (`->`, `!` and `!io` here), the lookahead (four characters here, one there), and the test names (lex/ident-io, lex/bang-alone, lex/arrow). One of the two drafts should point at the other. RFC 0014 open question 1 already proposes that the kernel's Lexical section become a pointer. (2) L10 keeps `->` and `!` as tokens that the grammar never uses. The only use of `!` is inside `!io`. This is the pattern RFC 0014 rejects, and it was one of the reasons RFC 0012 was rejected. (3) The Alternatives entry that rejects `io` as a reserved word gives RFC 0012 (rejected) as its reason. The header says this draft depends only on accepted RFCs, so the rationale must be restated without citing 0012. (4) Open question 1 ends mid-sentence. The draft also ends with empty 'Spec core', 'Findings' and 'Roadmap' headings. It is not complete enough to vote on. (5) Simplest fix for the effect marker: if the group keeps `!io`, remove `->` and `!` from L10 so the token set matches the grammar. If the group takes RFC 0014's `io` keyword, L11 and its four-character lookahead go away.

Cut E0003 and its parser-reported keyword rule. Rule 7 and the error table make `let let = 1` a special E0003 case, but rule 13 already says the parser reports E0100 at any token the grammar does not accept, and a keyword in a name position is exactly that. Dropping E0003 removes one error code, the table row, the sentence in rule 7, tests lex/ident-keyword.test and lex/ident-io.test, and open question 3, which only exists because E0003 sits in the wrong block. Codes are never reused, so nothing is lost by not assigning E0003. If the group wants a better message for keywords, that is a fix hint on E0100 (machine-applicable: rename the binding), not a new code.

Cut the Text bindings before adding anything. In the kernel a Text value can only be bound, assigned and printed, yet T3, the Text cases of B1 and B2, the E3 note and the kernel/text-bind test together spend a placement table and a test on it. Keep print of a text literal as the only Text form, and drop let and var of Text and assignment to a Text var. The Alternatives section already says the first programs need only Int and Text literals in print. Show the saving in Cost: the RFC gives no measured figure, and I have no benchmark finding that says Text bindings are used, so this cut rests on the RFC's own text.

Cut the CR LF line end. Remove the CRLF clause from rule 3, the CR exception in rule 2, and the run test `lex/ws-crlf.test`. This is open question 2. Principle 1 says one way to do each thing, and CR LF is a second spelling of a line end that every tool and formatter would have to normalise. Without it, rule 2 forbids every control character with no exception, and any CR is E0001 wherever it appears. That removes a clause, an exception and a test, and leaves one line-end rule: LF.

data.body: Coherence check against the constitution and the RFCs in rfcs/. (1) Conflict with constitution principle 1 (one way to do each thing, no optional syntax): B1 makes the `: T` annotation optional in `let` and `var`, so `let NAME = expr` and `let NAME: T = expr` are two ways to write one binding. F1 makes the result clause and `io` optional, and G4 makes `else` optional. Either justify each optional form against principle 1 or remove it. Simpler alternative for B1: drop the `: T` form, since the initialiser already fixes the binding type; the annotation only adds a mismatch check. (2) Reverses an idea that RFC 0013 rejected without answering its reason: TR3, the run-time step trap `step-exhausted`, is the 'fuel or step trap for non-terminating loops at run time' that rfcs/0013-kernel-v2.md rejected in its Alternatives section. This RFC answers RFC 0015's objection but not 0013's reason, which was that the trap is one the author did not write. Say why that reason no longer holds. (3) The kernel slot in architecture/ROADMAP.md (M2) names RFC 0003 as the kernel. 0003 is rejected lexical syntax, and the kernel lineage 0005, 0013 and 0015 is all rejected, so 0016 is the first kernel candidate. (4) Internal conflict between EX3 and TR3 on the step count and the limit; see the open issue filed with this comment. Dependencies RFC 0014 and RFC 0011 are accepted, so those pointers are valid.

Cut Text from the kernel. In this draft Text can only be bound, assigned and printed. Its restrictions (T3, the Text cases in E3 and P1, and the Text parameter and result ban in T6) exist to keep it from growing into a second value system. Removing it deletes T3, the Text form of print in P1 and P2, and the tests text-bind, print-text, err-text-op and err-text-param. print then takes one type, Int, so the compiler no longer picks a form by argument type. The cost is that text output moves to the later RFC that decides memory, which the Alternatives section already says Text depends on. The title would need to drop 'text output'. The rest of the kernel stays as drafted. I have not measured the token saving because spec/ is not in this checkout.

Cut `>` and `>=`. Write `b < a` and `b <= a` instead. Principle 1 (one way to do each thing) says two spellings of the same comparison are one too many. This removes two tokens from the grammar's `rel_expr` line, one clause from E4, and the matching cases from the operator table. Nothing in the test plan needs them: `arith.test` and `cmp-eq.test` use only `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`, `==` and `!=`. This is a principle-based cut, not a benchmark result; the checkout's bench/baselines holds only a README, so no measured finding supports keeping or dropping these operators.

Invalid UTF-8 (expected error, exit 1):
- U1 0xFF after two ASCII bytes: 61 62 ff 63 gives {E0001, 2, 3}.
- U2 lone continuation byte: 61 80 gives {E0001, 1, 2}.
- U3 overlong lead C0: c0 80 gives {E0001, 0, 1}.
- U4 offsets count bytes, not characters: c3 a9 ff gives {E0001, 2, 3}.
- U5 two bad bytes, first one reported: 61 ff ff gives {E0001, 1, 2}.

Byte order mark (expected error, exit 1):
- B1 at start: ef bb bf 61 gives {E0001, 0, 3}.
- B2 mid-file: 61 ef bb bf 62 gives {E0001, 1, 4}.

Control characters (expected error, exit 1):
- C1 NUL: 61 00 62 gives {E0001, 1, 2}.
- C2 U+001F: 61 1f 62 gives {E0001, 1, 2}.
- C3 DEL U+007F: 61 7f 62 gives {E0001, 1, 2}.
- C4 tab in code: 6c 65 74 09 61 gives {E0001, 3, 4}.
- C5 tab in a comment: 2f 2f 20 61 09 62 0a gives {E0001, 4, 5}.
- C6 tab in a text literal: 22 61 09 62 22 gives {E0001, 2, 3}.
- C7 DEL in a text literal: 22 7f 22 gives {E0001, 1, 2}.

Carriage return (expected error, exit 1):

- R2 CR at end of file: 61 0d gives {E0001, 1, 2}.
- R3 CR CR LF: 61 0d 0d 0a 62 gives {E0001, 1, 2}, because the first CR is not followed by LF.

Several errors in one file (smallest offset wins, expected exit 1):
- O1 tab at 2, invalid byte at 5: 61 62 09 63 64 ff gives {E0001, 2, 3}.
- O2 invalid byte at 0, tab at 3: ff 61 62 09 gives {E0001, 0, 1}.
- O3 tab at 0, BOM at 1: 09 ef bb bf gives {E0001, 0, 1}.

No test code is attached. The implementer writes source.test.ts from these rows.

Open points the RFC does not settle. No expected output is given for these, so no test is written:
1. A truncated sequence, such as e2 82 then LF or end of file, or c3 then 61. The RFC does not say whether the lead byte or the next byte is the first invalid byte.

The grammar accepts a bare IDENT as a primary, and accepted RFC 0014 rule 13 defines E0100 as a token the grammar does not accept, so an implementer cannot satisfy both. TR3 says calls are not counted, and the Alternatives section rejects counting calls. The 10000000-step example budget therefore has no single meaning. Fix these two and I will approve. The test gaps (no test for E4 non-Int comparisons, E5 non-Bool operands, or the combined `: R io` form in F1) are minor and can be added as new tests.

Architect coherence check. This is a comment, not a vote.

1. Conflict with the constitution, principle 3 (explicit effects). The constitution says whether a function can fail is visible in its signature. E9 and TR1 make overflow, divide-by-zero, stack-exhausted and step-exhausted traps that no signature shows. The `io` marker covers I/O only, so `fn div(a: Int, b: Int): Int` can fail and its signature says nothing. Either the signature has to show that a function can trap, or the RFC has to argue that the constitution's wording does not reach traps. As written, the merge bot would reject it under the constitution.

2. Local reasoning (principle 2). TR3 uses one run-wide step counter that is not reset when a function ends. Whether a call to `f` traps with step-exhausted then depends on loops run earlier in the program, not on the text of `f` or the signatures it references. That is the implicit global state principle 2 excludes. A budget that is local to a call, or that is part of the signature, would fit the principle. The RFC should say why it chose the shared counter over one of those.

3. Overlap with earlier kernel drafts. rfcs/0005-kernel.md, rfcs/0013-kernel-v2.md and rfcs/0015-kernel-v3.md are still status draft, and 0016 is the draft this RFC replaces. The RFC should say which of 0005, 0013 and 0015 it supersedes. Otherwise several kernel RFCs compete for one slot.

Architect coherence review. Three problems, one overlap check.

1. Conflicts with constitution principle 2 (local reasoning: no implicit global state). TR3 defines one loop counter per run that is 'not reset when a loop or function ends'. So whether a function traps depends on what ran before it. Example: main calls work() once, which runs 600 million while-condition evaluations and returns; a second call to work() traps with step-exhausted although its text is unchanged. The Alternatives section rejects a per-loop counter but does not address this global one. Use a budget per call or per example, or state the trade-off and why it is worth it.

2. Principle 3 (explicit effects: whether a function can 'fail' is 'visible in its signature'). The overflow, divide-by-zero, stack-exhausted and step-exhausted traps (E1, E2, TR1 to TR3) appear in no signature. The RFC never mentions principle 3 or argues the trade-off against principle 7. Add that argument to Alternatives, or show how a signature records these failures.

3. Test plan against the constitution's coverage rule (no grammar production without a conformance test). Nothing in the plan tests while_stmt (C3). The Text alternative of type (let and var annotations, T3) has no test. Motivation names kernel/example-call-ok.test, kernel/err-example-stack.test, kernel/err-example-budget.test and kernel/err-fn-print.test, but the plan does not list them, and the Coverage section it describes is missing. The plan also ends partway through the fn-void entry.

No overlap: RFCs 0005, 0013, 0015, 0016 and 0017 are all rejected, and no open RFC covers the same ground. I found no simpler alternative in the accepted spec. I found no contradiction between sections of this RFC.

Cut `!=`. `a != b` is `not (a == b)`, the same kind of synonym that RFC 0018 removes for `>`, `>=` and `<=`, so the same argument applies. Remove the `!=` alternative from `eq_expr`, change E3 to name only `==`, and write the `cmp-eq.test` line as `if not (1 == 2) { print(3) }`. This leaves one equality operator, matching the one ordering operator, and the grammar stays a single rule per meaning. Net: one production alternative and one token fewer, paid for by nothing the programmer loses.

Cut `Text` variables before adding anything. T3 lets `Text` appear in `let` and `var` initialisers and in assignments to a `Text` var, but the kernel gives `Text` no operation besides `print`, so those positions add no program that a literal argument to `print` cannot already write. Limit `Text` to a TEXT literal as the argument of `print`. That removes the Text cases of B1 and B2, the Text-typed binding and assignment rules that T3 and E0200 cover, and the `let`/`var` examples that use `Text`. Bring Text variables back in the RFC that gives `Text` a memory decision, which this RFC already defers.

Coherence check on RFC 0020 (kernel-v8). Three points, most serious first.

1. Conflict with the constitution, principle 3. Principle 3 says whether a function can fail must be visible in its signature. RFC 0020 keeps the four traps (overflow, divide-by-zero, stack-exhausted, step-exhausted; TR1 to TR3) out of signatures, and open question 1 calls this an exception. The constitution has no exception clause, and the merge bot rejects an RFC that conflicts with it regardless of votes. As drafted, the RFC cannot pass. The designers need either a signature-visible form of failure for the trapping operations, or a design in which those operations cannot fail (for example a checked result type). Choosing between them is for the designers and the votes.

2. Gap against constitution principle 5. Principle 5 says the compiler runs examples and fails the build if they do not hold. EX3 says `check` runs examples and `run` does not, and it says nothing about `build`. The RFC must state whether `build` evaluates examples. If it does not, principle 5 is not met.

3. Status of a cited dependency. The RFC calls RFC 0014 'accepted' and relies on that for its unchanged lex tests. The file rfcs/0014-lexical-syntax-v3.md says 'Status: draft'. Confirm 0014's status before the vote, or correct the citation.

Smaller: the `trap-step` row in the Test plan reads `while true { } }`, with an extra closing brace.

Checked and consistent: the comparison grammar against G6 and the precedence list; the trap names against RFC 0004 section 5; the trap-kind wording against RFC 0004's trap rule; and the expected outputs of arith, return-bare, fn-recursion and while-sum, which I worked out by hand.

Cut the Text binding forms. Keep Text only as the literal argument of print. Delete `let`/`var` with type `Text`, assignment to a Text var, and the Text clause of T3, so T3 becomes: Text may appear only as the argument of print. That lets `type` drop Text, and `ptype` and `rtype` merge into one rule over Int and Bool. The tests `text-bind`, `err-text-op` and the Text cases of `err-text-arg` go with it, and the card loses its Text-variable line. A program that prints the same string twice repeats the literal, which costs fewer tokens than the binding rules it needs. Estimated saving is about 100 tokens (not measured, since spec/ is absent).

Cut before adding anything: the Text special cases. Keep one rule, that Text may appear only in let/var initialisers, assignment to a Text var, and print (T3). Drop the T6 clause that makes a Text parameter or result E0100; under T3 it becomes E0200 like any other Text use. Drop the E3 sentence 'Text has no equality', since T3 already covers it. Delete the tests err-text-param, err-text-result and err-text-op, and keep err-text-arg as the one Text error test. Nothing in the RFC cites a benchmark finding that models need Text outside print, so these extra rules are not yet justified. Constitution principle 3 says failure shows in the signature. Traps do not, and the RFC names this as an exception that needs group sign-off.

I could not check this against spec/card.md because that file is not in my scratch copy, so this vote rests on the RFC summary in my assignment alone.

This draft says it does not amend RFC 0005 or 0006, both rejected, but never mentions 0020. Four clashes with 0020: (1) Rule 16 says MIN % -1 traps overflow; 0020 E2 says MIN % -1 is 0, and the test ints/mod-min.test would contradict 0020's trap-min-mod. (2) The precedence table in rule 12 puts == and != one level below < <= > >=; 0020 puts all six comparisons on one non-chaining level (G6). So 1 < 2 == true is valid here and E0100 under 0020. (3) Rule 24 exits with status 3; 0020 TR1 and RFC 0004 section 5 say status 1. (4) The trap kinds 'divide by zero' and 'byte out of range' do not match 0020's hyphenated kinds such as divide-by-zero. Overlap: the Issue #31 argument for E0200 is already settled, since 0020's diagnostic table uses E0200 for type mismatch; cite that rather than the E0102 block argument. Open questions 5 and 6 are answered by 0020: let is a statement (stmt, let_stmt) and print is built in (P1). Simpler option: keep only the new parts (the Byte type, the int and byte built-ins, and their E0300 names) as a delta on 0020, and drop the duplicate Int and Bool text and traps.

Conflicts with accepted RFC 0020 and with RFC 0004 section 4. (1) The header says RFC 0020 is extended by new rules only. But 0020 T6 says parameter and result types are Int or Bool, and T7 says any other name in a type position is E0100. This draft makes Arr<T> legal there and replaces 0020's type, ptype and rtype productions. That is an amendment of 0020, so it needs a kernel revision before acceptance, as the Cost section partly concedes. (2) RFC 0004 section 4 defines blocks only up to E0599. E0600 and E0601 fall in no block, so 'E0600 and E0601 are new' is not the whole check. E0601 is a missing-effect error and belongs in the effects block, E0400 to E0499, next to 0020's E0400. E0600 belongs in the types block. (3) The trap kinds 'index out of bounds' and 'out of memory' contain spaces. 0020 TR1 kinds are hyphenated (divide-by-zero, stack-exhausted), so use index-out-of-bounds and out-of-memory. (4) AR25 says the reserved names are 'as in RFC 0020 B5 and F6', but B5 reserves only print, Int, Bool and Text. These are new reservations, not the same rule. (5) The Motivation and open question 2 tie the Byte element to RFC 0009, which is rejected. The Byte type is now in draft RFC 0021, so point there. Simpler option: AR10 gives four contexts that can type array(). Requiring an annotation on the let or var that holds an empty array removes three of them and the context search with them, and the checklist does not need the rest.

It also restates Int and Bool rules that RFC 0020 already defines without saying so, and it calls E0200 and E0300 new, though RFC 0019 and RFC 0020 already use them for type mismatch and duplicate or reserved names. Trap exit status is 3, but accepted RFC 0020 TR1 says exit status 1 and RFC 0021 does not declare an amendment of TR1. Seven of its run tests expect exit 3, so they contradict the accepted kernel. Its test plan also claims every operator row is covered, but no test uses `*`, `<=`, `>=`, `not`, or `!=` on Int or Bool. The text calls E0200 and E0300 new and contested, but accepted RFC 0020 already uses both for the same meanings, which the open questions say must be checked. Would approve if the trap status is either changed to 1 or amended in writing with TR1 named, and tests are added for the missing operators.

The design fits the accepted kernel: trap status 1 matches RFC 0020 TR1, and E0600 and E0601 appear in no other RFC. The test plan cannot run as written, though. `copy-on-assign` and `return-param-copy` use names `a` that are never declared, `borrow-param` gives no program, and `err-missing-alloc` is an incomplete program. `trap-oom` relies on tens of millions of pushes with no stated runtime budget. Would approve once each test is a complete program with stated expected output, and the amendment question is settled.
